source.title: Towards strong pruning for lottery tickets with non-zero biases
source.authors: Jonas Fischer; A. Gadhikar; Rebekka Burkholz

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. Figure 4 values are not transcribed in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports pruning experiments and trainability results, but they concern finding untrained subnetworks by pruning, not gradient-based training from random initialization to low training classification error. Its results therefore do not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's CIFAR-10 edge-popup results measure the test performance of pruned, untrained tickets, not training classification error from gradient-based training. Its LeNet construction results report test accuracy of tickets approximating a separately trained target. These are outside the claim versions; cited prior work is not extracted as this paper's result.
record.test_reason: The study uses signal-preserving He and looks-linear initialization to develop strong lottery ticket pruning. Its results concern approximation, pruning performance and signal norms at initialization; they do not measure gradient-training error, training speed or maximum trainable depth. Section 3.2's signal-preservation analysis does not by itself test V4's learning outcomes.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors extend strong lottery ticket existence results and initialization schemes to nonzero biases, enabling universal approximation by pruning. Their signal-preservation analysis motivates trainability, and their pruning extensions improve synthetic-task results. CIFAR-10 pruning shows no significant advantage from nonzero biases; the authors leave open whether this reflects image tasks or limitations of current pruning algorithms.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates pruning randomly initialized networks to obtain untrained strong lottery tickets, with nonzero bias initialization and edge-popup variants. The claim versions concern gradient-based network training and training error.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that sparsity and the choice of bias initialization and parameter rescaling affect synthetic-task ticket performance. Its CIFAR-10 comparison reports no significant difference between zero- and nonzero-bias initializations.

fits_no_version.finding: Lemma 3.2 derives expected squared output norms for independent symmetric weight and bias distributions. Section 3.2 also extends looks-linear initialization to paired nonzero biases. Neither analysis measures learning speed or successful training depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Appropriately scaled nonzero biases can preserve initial signal magnitudes in the analyzed ReLU networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Nonzero-bias networks yield better untrained tickets on the two synthetic tasks, with an exception for unscaled edge-popup on the ellipse task at retained fraction 0.01. Parameter rescaling improves recovery at very low retained fractions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonzero-bias initialization and parameter rescaling can improve strong lottery ticket recovery on the tested synthetic tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix B.1 reports successful CIFAR-10 ticket pruning with both bias initializations and no significant difference in achieved performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonzero-bias initialization provides no demonstrated performance advantage for the tested CIFAR-10 strong lottery ticket pruning procedures.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports MNIST accuracies of 97.98%, 97.94% and 97.96% for constructed orthogonal, uniform and normal tickets, respectively, against 97.96% for the trained target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subset-sum construction can recover untrained tickets matching the tested MNIST target's accuracy under several nonzero-bias initializations.

record.code_released: Anonymized code is available to reviewers and will be made publicly available after publication; later text says all code and data publicly available. URL not stated.
record.problems: The CIFAR-10 results are presented only in Figure 4 without numeric values in the supplied text. Imaging experiments use 5 repetitions for classification and 4 for reconstruction, and the paper describes the zero- versus nonzero-bias results as not significantly different without reporting a test or p-value. The CIFAR-10 experiments evaluate ticket performance, not training classification error.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the paper's reported outcomes do not measure any claim version's named behavior. Figure 4 reports CIFAR-10 ticket results, but these are test task outcomes of pruned, untrained networks rather than training error after gradient-based training.

untested.parts: Training classification error of randomly initialized convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random labels and effects of size, stopping and regularization.
Frequency of spurious local minima and its reduction through extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student training.
Depth-dependent training degradation and its prevention through residual shortcuts, special initialization or Fixup.
Effects of initialization on actual gradient-training speed and trainable depth, including orthogonal-versus-Gaussian tanh training and very deep convolutional networks.
Loss recovery, divergence and sharpness dynamics relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Batch normalization's effects on accuracy gains and learning-rate tolerance, and corresponding Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Keeping the result rows empty is appropriate for these claim versions. Change the record's inconsistent tests/T6 classification to uses_without_test/T4. The paper's use of SGD or Adam to optimize pruning scores does not establish the named gradient-training outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: Whether gradient-based training from random initialization reaches near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted labels, and how model size, training duration, early stopping, or regularization affect that outcome.
Whether extra student width reduces spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Whether depth raises training error in plain networks and identity shortcuts, special initialization, or Fixup prevent that degradation.
Whether activation-matched initialization or orthogonal weights improve gradient-based training speed or trainable depth, including 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
Whether training above a stability threshold recovers or diverges, and how sharpness behaves during such training.
Whether batch normalization speeds accuracy gains or permits higher learning rates, and whether Fixup matches normalized residual networks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
